newsitem.title: GERMANY: Siemens computer unit sales rise 11 pct.
newsitem.headline: Siemens computer unit sales rise 11 pct.

text.p: German industrial giant Siemens AG said on Thursday its Siemens Nixdorf computer unit, aided by a rebound in Europe outside of Germany, saw worldwide sales rise 13 percent to 5.7 billion marks ($3.4 billion) in the first five months of business year 1996/97.
New orders in the period rose 14 percent to six billion marks, Gerhard Schulmeyer, Siemens Nixdorf Informationssysteme AG (SNI) chief executive, said at the CeBIT computer trade fair here.

In Germany, sales rose 11 percent to 3.5 billion marks and orders also increased 11 percent to 3.5 billion marks. Internationally, sales climbed 21 percent to 2.2 billion marks and orders 24 percent to 2.5 billion marks.

All of the figures take into account the loss of revenue from the sale of SNI's 900 million-mark high-end printer business last year. In 1995/96, which ended September 30, SNI sales rose seven percent to 13.9 billion marks. Net income was 29 million marks.
Much of the growth stemmed from the rest of Europe, where Italian sales in the five-month period increased 36 percent, Austrian sales rose 25 percent and French sales rose 19 percent.
Despite the European recovery, Siemens Nixdorf was concentrating on growing sales in Asia and the United States, Schulmeyer said.

"European is under-investing in technology, compared to the rest of the world," he said at a news conference, adding that SNI expected the European market to grow 7.5 percent this year -- half the level of growth in Asian and the U.S.
The U.S. has 30.3 million computer users conected to the Internet, three times as many as Europe, he said.
In particular, Schulmeyer said SNI was trying to shift focus away from Germany, which spends $1,000 per worker on computer gear, half the level of the U.S.
"We are doing a good job in Asia but we are still heavily weighted toward Germany," he said.
At the same time, SNI was implementing a drastic reorganisation to break the company up into more than 250 units repsponsible for profit for different product lines in different countries.
"We have to learn to live with and like complexity," he said. "There is a massive shift in how you run companies. There is a shift to organisations that are dynamic and flexible."
